Every distribution in R has four functions: `d` (density or mass), `p` (CDF), `q` (quantile) and `r` (random draws). The distributions below come back all term: the binomial and Poisson in GLMs (sessions 9–12), the normal in linear and mixed models (sessions 5–8 and 15–19), the exponential and gamma in GLMs and survival (session 28).

```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## d, p, q, r

```{r dpqr}
dnorm(0)                      # density of N(0, 1) at 0 = 1/sqrt(2 pi)
pnorm(1.96) - pnorm(-1.96)    # P(|Z| < 1.96)
qnorm(0.975)                  # the 1.96 itself

dbinom(3, size = 10, prob = 0.2)   # P(Y = 3), Y ~ Bin(10, 0.2)
ppois(2, lambda = 4)               # P(Y <= 2), Y ~ Poisson(4)
qexp(0.5, rate = 1/3)              # median of Exp(mean 3) = 3 log 2
pgamma(2, shape = 2, rate = 1)     # P(Y <= 2), Y ~ Gamma(shape 2, rate 1)
```

## Mean and variance by simulation

| Distribution | Mean | Variance |
|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli($\pi$) | $\pi$ | $\pi(1-\pi)$ |
| Bin($m$, $\pi$) | $m\pi$ | $m\pi(1-\pi)$ |
| Poisson($\lambda$) | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ |
| Exponential(rate $\lambda$) | $1/\lambda$ | $1/\lambda^2$ |
| Gamma(shape $\alpha$, rate $\lambda$) | $\alpha/\lambda$ | $\alpha/\lambda^2$ |

```{r moments}
set.seed(2027)
B <- 1e5
sims <- list(
  bernoulli   = rbinom(B, size = 1, prob = 0.3),
  binomial    = rbinom(B, size = 10, prob = 0.2),
  poisson     = rpois(B, lambda = 4),
  exponential = rexp(B, rate = 1/3),
  gamma       = rgamma(B, shape = 2, rate = 0.5)
)
theory <- rbind(c(0.3, 0.21), c(2, 1.6), c(4, 4), c(3, 9), c(4, 8))
sim <- t(sapply(sims, function(s) c(mean(s), var(s))))
out <- round(cbind(sim, theory), 2)
colnames(out) <- c("sim mean", "sim var", "mean", "var")
out
```

The exponential is the gamma with shape $\alpha = 1$. For the gamma the variance is $\mu^2/\alpha$, so it grows with the square of the mean. That is the mean–variance relationship of the Gamma GLM (session 9).

## Real counts: great discoveries per year

`discoveries` (package `datasets`) counts the "great" inventions and scientific discoveries in each year from 1860 to 1959 ($n = 100$). If the counts were Poisson, the mean and the variance would be close.

```{r discoveries}
y <- as.numeric(discoveries)
c(n = length(y), mean = mean(y), var = var(y), ratio = var(y) / mean(y))

obs <- table(factor(y, levels = 0:12))
expected <- length(y) * dpois(0:12, lambda = mean(y))
round(rbind(observed = obs, poisson = expected), 1)
```

The variance (5.08) is larger than the mean (3.1), and the Poisson fit expects 4.5 years with no discovery where 9 were observed. Variance larger than the mean is overdispersion; we model it in session 10.

## Random vectors: $\mathbb E[AY] = A\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(AY) = A\Sigma A^\top$

Simulate a bivariate normal with `MASS::mvrnorm()` and check the two rules. Take $\mu = (1, 2)^\top$, $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2\\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, so $AY = (Y_1 + Y_2,\ Y_1 - Y_2)^\top$.

```{r mvn}
library(MASS)
mu    <- c(1, 2)
Sigma <- matrix(c(4, 2,
                  2, 3), nrow = 2)
A     <- matrix(c(1,  1,
                  1, -1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

drop(A %*% mu)             # theory: E[AY]
A %*% Sigma %*% t(A)       # theory: Var(AY)

set.seed(2027)
Y  <- mvrnorm(1e5, mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)   # n x 2, one draw per row
AY <- Y %*% t(A)                             # each row is (A y_i)^T
round(colMeans(AY), 2)
round(var(AY), 2)
```

Note the transpose: draws are stored as rows, so the transformation is `Y %*% t(A)`.

## Law of large numbers

```{r lln, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=6}
set.seed(2027)
x <- rexp(5000, rate = 1/3)
plot(cumsum(x) / seq_along(x), type = "l", log = "x",
     xlab = "n", ylab = "running mean")
abline(h = 3, lty = 2)
```

## Central limit theorem

Means of $n = 30$ draws from a skewed exponential are close to normal, with standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

```{r clt, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=6}
set.seed(2027)
means <- replicate(10000, mean(rexp(30, rate = 1/3)))
hist(means, breaks = 50, freq = FALSE, main = "", xlab = "sample mean (n = 30)")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 3, sd = 3 / sqrt(30)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
c(sd_sim = sd(means), sd_theory = 3 / sqrt(30))
```
